text: Do you know the biggest telescope in space had to be folded up like origami, just to fit inside its rocket?
This is the James Webb Space Telescope, built from NASA's own 3D model.
Its mirror is six and a half metres wide. Eighteen hexagons of beryllium, coated in gold.
Gold reflects infrared light. And Webb sees in infrared, the faint heat glow of the first galaxies.
But to see faint heat, the telescope itself must stay colder than minus two hundred and twenty degrees Celsius.
So it hides behind a huge sunshield. Five layers, each about a tenth of a millimetre thick.
On Christmas Day, twenty twenty-one, an Ariane five rocket launched it, folded tight.
Then, on the way, it unfolded itself. The sunshield, the mirror wings, piece by piece.
Engineers counted three hundred and forty-four steps that each had to work. With no backup.
Today, it works about one and a half million kilometres from Earth. No astronaut can go there to repair it.
Each mirror segment is lined up to within fifty nanometres. More than a thousand times thinner than a hair.
Webb looks very far away. Orbi Transfer looks close by.
Nearby shows files shared in your area, live, within about a second. Others only ever see the rough area.
